ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Andrew, the absent-minded mountain climber, climbed a mountain range, with a profile as shown in Figure 1 from point $P$ to point $Q$. From time to time he had to turn back to find bits of his equipment that he had dropped. The graph of the height $H$ of his position at time $t$ is shown in Figure 2 to the same scale as Figure 1. How many times did he turn back?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: Figure 1 shows the mountain profile from P to Q. Starting at P, the path rises steeply to a high peak, falls steeply to a valley, rises a short distance to a smaller peak, and then descends gently for a long distance to Q. Figure 2 shows Andrew's height H over time t on the same scale: it begins at height 0, has several rising and falling straight-line pieces, includes a flat horizontal piece near the end, and finally descends to height 0. Then reason: Since the two figures use the same scale, each sloping piece of the height-time graph can be matched to a corresponding sloping piece of the mountain profile, either in the forward direction from P to Q or in the reverse direction back toward P. Starting from P and tracing the graph forward, the first reverse-travel interval occurs on the initial steep slope before the high peak. A second reverse interval appears around the valley/smaller-peak part of the profile. A third reverse interval occurs on the final descending slope before the last movement to Q. The horizontal flat segment near the end is not a backward traverse; it only means his height stayed constant. Therefore the number of times he turned back is 3.

method.method_draft: Use a tracing/overlay reconstruction. First read Figure 1 as the actual mountain profile from P to Q: a steep rise from P to the high peak, a steep fall to a valley, a short rise to a smaller peak, and a long gentle fall to Q. Then read Figure 2 from left to right as Andrew's height history. Because the two figures are drawn to the same scale, each sloping piece of Figure 2 can be laid onto a matching piece of the Figure 1 profile, either in the forward direction toward Q or in the reverse direction back toward P. Start at P moving forward. Follow the height graph and mark any maximal interval that can only be matched by traversing the corresponding terrain segment in reverse. The first reverse interval occurs on the initial steep slope before the high peak, another occurs around the smaller peak/valley part, and another occurs on the final descending slope before the last descent to Q. The flat segment near the end is just staying at the same height and is not a backward traverse. Count the reverse-travel intervals: 3.

method.method_draft: Use a slope-sign classification. From Figure 1, list the possible forward terrain pieces: steep uphill from P, steep downhill from the first peak, moderate uphill to the second peak, and gentle downhill to Q. With the same scale, a segment of Figure 2 with the same slope sign and steepness as one of these forward pieces means Andrew is moving toward Q on that piece; a segment with the opposite sign for the matching terrain piece means he is retracing his path. Scan Figure 2 segment by segment and label each as forward, backward, or stationary. Merge consecutive segments with the same direction label. The backward labels occur in three separate blocks, while the other slope changes correspond to normal mountain peaks/valleys or a stationary flat part. Therefore Andrew turned back 3 times.

图像描述：Figure 1 shows the mountain profile from P to Q as four straight terrain pieces: a steep uphill from P to the first peak, a steep downhill to a valley, a moderate uphill to a second peak, and then a gentle downhill to Q. Figure 2 shows Andrew's height H against time t on the same grid scale, with several sloping pieces and one flat stationary piece near the end.

推理：Using the slope-sign classification, forward motion toward Q can only have the four Figure 1 slope types: steep up, steep down, moderate up, and gentle down. If a segment in Figure 2 has the opposite slope for the matching terrain piece, Andrew is retracing his route. Scanning Figure 2 from left to right: the initial steep rise is forward; the next reverse-slope part is backward, giving the first turnback block. Later, after forward motion over the first peak/valley, another opposite-slope segment appears on the steep downhill terrain, giving a second backward block. Farther along, after forward progress toward the later part of the route, another retracing segment appears before he resumes forward progress; this is the third backward block. The remaining slope changes are caused by ordinary peaks/valleys in the mountain profile or by the flat stationary part, not by additional turnbacks. Thus there are three separate backward blocks.
